Jamie Author on Keeping an Almanac

A novelist, almanac-keeper and video host talks about weather records, small towns, and why an almanac is a kind of diary.

By Alex Reporter — June 10, 2025

Welcome back to Writers at Work, our interview column with authors on the ideas that keep them writing. Our previous conversations were with a river poet and a map maker.

Jamie Author has written four novels, kept a handwritten almanac of her village for eighteen years, and hosts a long-running video series, Twelve Evenings, in which she visits a different small town each month and asks the oldest resident to describe the weather of their childhood.

Her new book, The Lantern Almanac, collects a decade of those records, rain and frost and first swallows, alongside the stories people told her while she wrote them down.

Alex Reporter: You have written novels, kept an almanac, and hosted a show. How do you introduce yourself?

Jamie Author: Usually as a record keeper. The novels, the almanac and the show are three ways of writing things down before they are forgotten. I started the almanac first, the novels came later, and the show happened almost by accident, when a neighbour filmed one of my visits.

Why an almanac? Most writers keep a diary.

An almanac is a diary that refuses to talk about you. It records the first frost, the height of the river, the day the swifts leave. After a few years you notice that it tells you more about yourself than a diary ever did, because you can see what you chose to notice.

How did The Lantern Almanac become a book?

Slowly. An editor saw a page of it pinned to the wall of a café, and asked whether there were more. There were eighteen notebooks. We chose ten years, cut the entries that only mattered to me, and kept the ones where somebody else’s voice came through.

Your show, Twelve Evenings, has run for more than a hundred episodes. What have you learned from it?

That everyone remembers weather. People who cannot tell you what year they married can tell you exactly how deep the snow was on the morning they left home. The weather is the frame, and the story is always about something else.

Do you worry that the places you record are disappearing?

Less than I used to. The villages change, but people keep noticing things. My job is to give them a page to write it on, and to keep turning up, month after month, until the page is full.

Jamie Author

What are you writing now?

A fifth novel, set in a lighthouse, told entirely through the keeper’s logbook. It is, I admit, another almanac in disguise.
